setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and have a long list of tasks for today.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are planning a day with more tasks than usual.
pressure: {coworker3} says to just start at the top of the list and keep going.
You have already lost 20 minutes to a late start.
detail: The list is written on the whiteboard.
Your lunch break is at noon.

tiers.1: The task with the nearest fixed deadline has to come first.
tiers.2: Work that is blocked should be moved, not waited on.
tiers.3: A large task due later needs a start today.
tiers.4: Protecting focused time makes every task faster.
tiers.5: Grouping similar tasks saves time once the order is set.

fact: One task on the list is due to a {client} by 10 a.m.
clear: You finished the 10 a.m. task before leaving yesterday.
issues.done: the 10 a.m. task is already finished
issues.action: Do the task that is due at 10 a.m. first.
issues.reason: A fixed deadline in a few hours outranks tasks with more time. Missing it affects a {client}.
issues.lesson: Put the tasks with the nearest fixed deadlines first.

shortcut.text: Start with the quick, easy tasks to build momentum.
shortcut.why: Easy tasks feel productive, but they can push the urgent task past its deadline.
shortcut.mis: Easy tasks first is always efficient.

fact: One task cannot start until {coworker} sends a file this afternoon.
clear: {coworker} already sent the file you were waiting for.
issues.action: Move that task to the afternoon and work on tasks you can do now.
issues.brief: move it later and do what you can now
issues.reason: Waiting on a blocked task wastes the morning. Reordering keeps you productive.
issues.lesson: Plan around blocked tasks instead of waiting on them.

shortcut.text: Wait at your desk until {coworker} sends the file.
shortcut.why: Waiting all morning wastes time that other tasks could use.
shortcut.mis: You should do tasks strictly in list order.

fact: A large task due Friday has not been started yet.
issues.action: Break the large task into steps and schedule the first step today.
issues.brief: break it into steps and start one today
issues.reason: Large tasks left until the end become rushed. Small scheduled steps make Friday realistic.
issues.lesson: Break big tasks into steps and start them early.

shortcut.text: Leave the large task until Thursday, when there is more time.
shortcut.why: Waiting until Thursday leaves no room for problems.
shortcut.mis: Big tasks are best done all at once at the end.

clear: You already broke the Friday task into steps and scheduled them this week.
issues.done: the large task is already broken into scheduled steps

fact: Messages keep interrupting you every few minutes.
issues.action: Set aside blocks of focused time and check messages between them.
issues.reason: Constant switching slows every task. Checking at set times keeps you responsive and focused.
issues.lesson: Protect focused time by handling messages in batches.

shortcut.text: Answer every message the moment it arrives.
shortcut.why: Answering instantly breaks your focus every few minutes.
shortcut.mis: Instant replies are always the most productive.

fact: Three small tasks on the list all need {equipment|the} set up.
issues.short: the three tasks that share a setup
issues.action: Group the three tasks so {equipment|the} is set up only once.
issues.reason: Setting up once instead of three times saves real time.
issues.lesson: Group tasks that share setup or tools.

shortcut.text: Do the three tasks at different times as they come up on the list.
shortcut.why: Setting up three separate times wastes effort.
shortcut.mis: Task order on the list is the most efficient order.

proceed.text: Work through the tasks in order of importance and deadline.
proceed.why: Nothing on the list needs special handling, so working by importance and deadline is the efficient plan.
proceed.lesson: Order work by importance and deadline, and adjust as things change.

generic.text: Spend the first hour making a detailed color-coded schedule.
generic.why: A short plan helps, but an hour of planning eats time the tasks need.
generic.mis: More planning always means more productivity.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to take half of your list without checking with {lead|the}.
generic.why: Shifting work without checking can overload a coworker and confuse the plan.
generic.mis: Handing off work is the fastest fix for a full list.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to rank every task for you before starting.
overcaution.why: The priorities are clear. Asking the lead to rank everything delays the start.
overcaution.mis: Only a supervisor can set your priorities.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, organizing a full day of tasks.

due10: Something on the list is due to a {client} this morning.
large: A big task due later this week has not been started.
batch: Several small tasks need the same equipment.

steps.text: List every task with its deadline
Group the tasks that share a setup
Split the big task into steps
Work through the rest of the plan
Review what is left at the end of the day

rel: You need the full list to confirm what is most urgent.
The deadline task comes before the rest.
Grouping happens once you see all the tasks.
Grouped tasks are planned before you start them.
You see the big task when you list everything.
The first step of the big task goes into today's plan.
You review once the work is done.
process.lesson: List everything, handle deadlines, organize the rest, work, then review.

title: Your plan for today
intro: You drafted today's plan. Check it before you start.
doc.lesson: An efficient plan puts fixed deadlines first and works around blocked tasks.

lines.text: 8:00 - Finish the {client} task due at 10 a.m.
9:30 - Set up {equipment|the} and do all three tasks that need it.
lines.fine: Groups tasks that share a setup.

bad.text: 9:30 - Set up {equipment|the} for one task; set it up again at 1:00 and 3:00 for the others.
bad.why: Setting up three times wastes time when the tasks could be grouped.

lines.text: 11:00 - First step of the large Friday task.

bad.text: 11:00 - Leave the large Friday task until Thursday night.
bad.why: Waiting until the last night leaves no room for problems.

lines.text: 1:00 - Task that needs {coworker}'s file, which arrives after lunch.
lines.fine: Schedules the blocked task after the file arrives.

bad.text: 8:00 - Task that needs {coworker}'s file, which arrives this afternoon.
bad.why: The file will not arrive until the afternoon, and 8:00 is already set aside for the 10 a.m. deadline.

bad.text: Answer every message the moment it arrives, all day.

lines.text: 4:30 - Review what is left and plan tomorrow.

bad.text: 4:30 - Leave without checking what is left.
bad.why: Skipping the review means unfinished tasks are forgotten.

review.notes: Prioritization by deadline, dependency and effort.

kits.familyName: Using people, tools and materials well
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. {Lead|the} asked you and the team to finish a large job for a {client} by tomorrow.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are coordinating today's work on a big job for a {client}.
pressure: {coworker3} says the fastest way is to just throw everything at it.
The job is the biggest one this month.
detail: The team has four people today.
The work area is clean and ready.

tiers.1: Equipment that is failing has to be dealt with before it wastes the whole order.
tiers.2: Matching tasks to people's skills makes the team faster.
tiers.3: Materials wasted now cost money the order cannot recover.
tiers.4: Idle time is a resource too.
tiers.5: Saving energy is worthwhile once the work is organized.

fact: {Equipment|the} has started making a grinding noise and slowing down.
issues.action: Stop using {equipment|the} and report the noise to {lead|the} so it can be checked.
issues.brief: stop and report the equipment noise
issues.reason: Running failing equipment can break it completely and ruin work in progress. Reporting it early protects the order.
issues.lesson: Care for equipment by reporting problems before they become breakdowns.

shortcut.text: Keep running it until the order is done, then report it.
shortcut.brief: run it until the order is done
shortcut.why: Failing equipment can break mid-order and damage more work.
shortcut.mis: Equipment problems can wait until the job is finished.

fact: {coworker} is fastest at the detailed step, but has been assigned to stocking.
issues.action: Suggest switching assignments so {coworker} does the detailed step.
issues.brief: suggest moving {coworker} to the detailed step
issues.reason: Putting people where their skills fit speeds up the whole team.
issues.lesson: Use people's strengths when assigning work.

shortcut.text: Keep the assignments, since changing them might upset people.
shortcut.why: A quick, respectful suggestion is unlikely to upset anyone and saves real time.
shortcut.mis: Assignments should never change once made.

fact: You notice the team is opening new {supply.plural} while half-used ones sit on the shelf.
issues.action: Point out the half-used {supply.plural} and suggest using those first.
issues.reason: Using what is already open saves materials and money without slowing the work.
issues.lesson: Use materials fully before opening new ones.

shortcut.text: Ignore it, since new {supply.plural} are faster to grab.
shortcut.why: Small waste repeated across a big order adds up.

fact: {coworker2} is waiting with nothing to do until the next batch is ready.
issues.action: Suggest {coworker2} prepare the labels for the next batch while waiting.
issues.reason: Idle time is a lost resource. Useful prep work keeps the whole order moving.
issues.lesson: Find useful work for idle time.

shortcut.text: Let {coworker2} wait, since the batch will be ready soon.
shortcut.why: Waiting time adds up across the day when useful prep work is available.

fact: Two machines in the area are running even though nobody is using them.
issues.action: Switch off the unused machines, following their normal shutdown steps.
issues.reason: Idle machines waste energy and add wear for no benefit.
issues.lesson: Conserve energy by switching off equipment that is not in use.

shortcut.text: Leave them running, since turning them back on takes time.
shortcut.why: If they are not needed, leaving them on only wastes energy.
shortcut.mis: Equipment should always stay on in case it is needed.

proceed.text: Keep the team working through the order as planned.
proceed.why: People, equipment and materials are being used well, so the plan should continue.
proceed.lesson: When resources are used well, keep the work moving as planned.

generic.text: Ask {lead|the} to bring in extra staff right away.
generic.why: Extra staff costs money and may not be needed if current resources are used well.
generic.mis: More people always means faster work.

generic.why: Ordering extra without checking needs ties up money and space.
